Overview

Abuja as a Business Centre

Abuja is the capital of Nigeria and the centre of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), created in 1976 to replace Lagos as the seat of government. The territory is divided into six area councils, Abaji, Abuja Municipal, Bwari, Gwagwalada, Kuje and Kwali, and is run by the Federal Capital Territory Administration under a minister appointed by the President, with the Federal Capital Development Authority responsible for infrastructure. The National Bureau of Statistics put the FCT population at about 4.35 million in 2018, with growth far above the national rate and much of it in satellite settlements. Real estate, construction, services and government spending drive the local economy, and Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport is the country's second-busiest.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Abuja because so many decisions with commercial consequences are made there: federal contracts and concessions, licences and permits, regulatory approvals and appointments to state-owned bodies. Foreign investors, lenders and contractors need to know who stands behind an Abuja-based counterparty, whether intermediaries offering access to ministries or agencies have relevant connections that create bribery risk, and whether a politically exposed person is involved. Abuja's property market, built on allocated land titles administered by the FCT, raises its own questions about title validity and beneficial ownership. Litigation before the federal courts sitting in Abuja is another frequent source of research needs.

Typical Matters

Investigative Work Connected to Abuja

01

Federal procurement and contractor diligence

Research on contractors, consortium partners and subcontractors bidding for or performing federal and FCT contracts, covering corporate registration, ownership, prior contract performance, published procurement disputes and litigation, so clients can assess whether a partner is capable and free of reported integrity concerns.

02

Intermediary and agent risk

Background research on consultants, agents and introducers in Abuja who offer access to ministries, agencies or state-owned companies, examining their business history, relationships with officials disclosed in public sources and any reported involvement in corruption investigations, to support anti-bribery compliance decisions.

03

Politically exposed person research

Reputation and background research on serving and former federal officials, legislators and their associates, drawing on public appointments, Code of Conduct and court records, media reporting and corporate filings, to inform onboarding, partnership and investment decisions where a politically exposed person is a shareholder, director or beneficiary.

04

Abuja land title verification

Factual research supporting counsel on Abuja property transactions and disputes, covering the history of allocations, certificates of occupancy, consents to assign or mortgage, competing claims and litigation, given recurring concerns about undocumented estates, uncollected titles and revocations in the FCT.

05

Federal court litigation research

Identifying and summarising litigation involving a counterparty before the Federal High Court, the High Court of the FCT and the Court of Appeal in Abuja, including disputes with regulators and federal agencies, to support due diligence, dispute strategy and enforcement planning.

Local Context

Courts, Records and Institutions in Abuja

Federal courts in the capital

The Federal High Court has its headquarters on Shehu Shagari Way in Abuja's Central District. It hears civil and criminal matters within section 251 of the 1999 Constitution, including many company and federal regulatory cases, and has coordinate jurisdiction with the High Court of the FCT, which hears general civil and criminal matters in the territory. The Court of Appeal has an Abuja division. Court files are held by each court rather than in a central searchable database.

FCT land administration and AGIS

Land in the FCT is allocated by the FCT Administration and administered through Abuja Geographic Information Systems (AGIS), which handles applications, certificates of occupancy, title registration, legal searches, ministerial consents to assign or mortgage, and recertification of older titles. In August 2026 the minister's office reported signing 26,272 certificates of occupancy over three years. Formal legal searches at AGIS, made through counsel, are the starting point for verifying a property's history.

FCT administration and development

The Federal Capital Territory Administration, headed by a minister, governs the territory through secretariats including area council services, while the Federal Capital Development Authority, created in 1976, delivers infrastructure under the Abuja Master Plan of 1979. Rapid growth has outpaced the plan, producing informal settlements, resettlement and compensation programmes and disputes over demolitions and land swaps. These programmes can affect the security of title and the value of development land.

Federal institutions and procurement

As the seat of government, Abuja hosts the federal ministries, departments and agencies whose contracts, licences and approvals drive much commercial activity across Nigeria, as well as the Bureau of Public Procurement, which oversees federal procurement. Federal anti-corruption bodies described on the Nigeria country page operate at national level. Published procurement notices, court cases and agency announcements are useful public sources when reviewing an Abuja counterparty's dealings with government.

Engagement Standard

How TDSC Scopes Matters in Abuja

TDSC scopes Abuja matters from Nashville and begins with the decision the client faces: entering a contract with a government-facing counterparty, acquiring property, onboarding a politically exposed person or litigating before the federal courts. Research draws on Corporate Affairs Commission filings and the persons with significant control register, reported judgments, procurement and agency publications, and Nigerian and international media. Land title questions are handled through formal AGIS searches made by Nigerian counsel. Because Nigeria has no dedicated investigator licensing regime, any local enquiry is scoped with counsel and excludes surveillance and any attempt to obtain official records outside lawful process. TDSC has no office in Abuja.

TDSC has no office in Abuja. Engagements are directed from Nashville, Tennessee; where work on the ground is needed, it is performed by appropriately licensed local professionals under a written scope.

Questions

Abuja: Frequently Asked Questions

Does TDSC have staff in Abuja?

No. TDSC has no office, staff or address in Nigeria. Engagements touching Abuja are scoped and managed from Nashville. Where a matter requires document retrieval, a formal land search or enquiries in the capital, TDSC works with qualified Nigerian counsel or professionals identified with the client under a written scope.

How can an Abuja property title be checked?

Titles in the FCT are administered through Abuja Geographic Information Systems. A legal search through counsel can confirm the registered holder, the certificate of occupancy, any consents to assign or mortgage and recorded encumbrances. TDSC complements this with research on the history of the allocation, related litigation and the parties involved, but does not give legal opinions on title.

Can TDSC tell us whether an intermediary has government connections?

TDSC can research what public sources show: an intermediary's corporate interests, directorships, prior roles, family or business links reported in the media and any litigation or investigations. It does not use non-public government data. The findings help compliance teams decide whether the relationship needs enhanced controls or should not proceed.

Which courts in Abuja hear commercial disputes?

Company and many federal regulatory matters are heard by the Federal High Court, headquartered in Abuja, while general civil disputes in the territory go to the High Court of the FCT. Appeals go to the Court of Appeal, which has an Abuja division. Records are held by each court, so research combines reported judgments, registry enquiries through counsel and press coverage.

Is politically exposed person research lawful in Nigeria?

Research using lawfully available public information is generally permissible, but processing personal data must comply with the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023. TDSC documents the purpose and lawful basis for each engagement, limits collection to what the decision requires and secures the results. Surveillance and attempts to obtain bank, telecoms or police records are excluded.
